summary: This benchmark presents a rigorous differential analysis of HTTP Range request handling across seven widely used static-file server implementations, evaluating 58 test cases against RFC 9110 specifications. The findings reveal substantial divergence in behavior across servers, including non-compliant suffix handling, malformed Content-Range responses in Go, and an npm packaging discrepancy in range-parser. The methodology is well-isolated and thorough, providing actionable insights for HTTP client and server developers.
strengths: Systematic and reproducible differential testing methodology applying 58 raw byte-level test vectors across seven distinct web server/framework implementations.
Careful mapping to RFC 9110 specification requirements, categorizing responses rigorously into prescribed, permitted, lenient, rejected, and non-compliant behaviors.
Discovery of concrete edge-case defects and discrepancies, notably the npm packaging mismatch in range-parser 1.3.0 (PR #66) and Go's invalid Content-Range generation on zero-length ranges.
Comprehensive tabular breakdown in the appendix providing clear, granular visibility into server disagreement patterns.
weaknesses: Testing is limited to a single 100-byte file and an empty file over GET requests, leaving out large multi-megabyte files, conditional headers (If-Range), and HEAD requests.
Evaluation tests only a single pinned version per ecosystem without evaluating how intermediate reverse proxies or CDNs might alter the headers before reaching the framework handler.
No external standalone server daemons (e.g., Nginx, Apache HTTP Server, Caddy) were included alongside the application framework handlers.
suggestions: Expand test cases to include If-Range and precondition interaction, as clients often pair Range headers with validators.
Include standalone web servers (e.g., Nginx, Caddy, Apache httpd) to compare framework static-file helpers against production reverse-proxy baselines.
Submit upstream bug reports for verified non-conformance issues, particularly Go's malformed Content-Range values and range-parser's npm release mismatch.

claims.text: RFC 9110 Section 14: a server MUST ignore an unknown range unit
A suffix longer than the file selects the whole file [per RFC 9110 Section 14.1.2]

Git tag v1.3.0 points to the merge of #66, 'Clamp a suffix whose length exceeds the representation' (2026-06-25), whose index.js uses Math.max(size - end, 0). The npm tarball of range-parser 1.3.0 records gitHead 855f5b1f
Go's httpservecontentmaxranges GODEBUG setting has an old value of 1 for modules declaring a Go version before 1.26

novelty_vs_existing.title: The HTTP Garden: Discovering Parsing Vulnerabilities in HTTP/1.1 Implementations by Differential Fuzzing of Request Streams
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: While HTTP Garden applied differential testing to HTTP framing and chunked transfer parsing, this submission targets HTTP Range request parsing and byte-window semantics across application frameworks.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Who's Breaking the Rules? Studying Conformance to the HTTP Specifications and its Security Impact
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Rautenstrauch & Stock checked conformance against high-level RFC rules with minimal probe variants, whereas this benchmark explores a dense 58-probe matrix specifically exercising Range boundary conditions, suffixes, and numeral parsing.
